claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with distinct phase domains and interfacial regions.
In situ diffraction peak-position shifts can be used to measure lattice-strain evolution during mechanical loading.
Microbeam diffraction mapping can spatially resolve strain differences among the heterostructural domains of HfNbTiVAl10.
Microbeam diffraction can deconvolute overlapping diffraction signals from different heterostructural domains.
Applied tensile loading induces differential lattice-strain responses at heterostructural interfaces and phase domains.
The slope of lattice strain versus applied stress during elastic deformation determines plane-specific diffraction elastic constants.
Diffraction elastic-constant relationships can connect measured lattice strain to the global Young's modulus of HfNbTiVAl10.
The temporal and spatial distribution of lattice strain directly correlates with the yield behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
The temporal and spatial distribution of lattice strain directly correlates with fracture initiation and fracture-related behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
Localized lattice-strain anomalies precede fracture initiation and can be used to identify it rapidly.
The diffraction-based approach can provide a direct, real-time measure of elastic response.
The diffraction-based approach can directly measure plastic yielding and fracture initiation.
The approach will improve predictive precision by at least approximately 25% relative to established simulation methods.
The approach will reduce computational time and overhead relative to full atomistic simulations or conventional finite-element models.
Established atomistic and conventional finite-element simulations have lower predictive accuracy for heterogeneous multiphase materials.
The method may fail if diffraction signals from overlapping domains cannot be resolved adequately.
Extreme heterogeneity or unforeseen phase transformations may cause measured lattice strains not to represent localized mechanical responses reliably.

Failure to predict independently measured Young's modulus within 25% error and yield strength within 15% error, or failure to find a consistent strain-anomaly/fracture correlation, is the predeclared falsification result.
